text.tspan: Everyday English - C1 - 2026/10/04 - Essay - 01
Readers spend time with books.
Pexels · 6344242
A little time to read
The decision to read a short book may appear ordinary, yet it exposes a recurring tension between arrangements that make life manageable and
experiences that resist being prescribed. A defensible approach combines proportionate preparation with a willingness to reconsider whose interests a
plan serves.
Preparation has value because a small reading goal is easier to keep than an ambitious one. In the present case, we read five pages after lunch rather
than wait for a free afternoon. Such an intervention is modest, but that modesty is its strength: it removes a foreseeable obstacle without claiming to
determine the entire experience. Structure is useful to the extent that it releases attention rather than consuming it.
That argument requires a qualification, however: discussing an idea helps us understand it more clearly. For instance, we explain a favourite passage to a
friend and listen to a different interpretation. An arrangement that appears efficient from one standpoint may impose costs elsewhere. Listening to those
affected is therefore not an optional gesture of goodwill; it supplies information without which the plan cannot be adequately evaluated.
The resulting principle is one of proportion. Preparation deserves support when it clarifies responsibilities and protects time, while responsiveness
prevents it from hardening into an end in itself. To judge the experience well is to examine both what the arrangement enables and what it may
inadvertently exclude.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion. Each body paragraph
needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a new proposal.
Persuade a group to change how they read a short book. Support your recommendation with two different reasons and a practical example of each. Use
four short paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion. (Model: One possible outline: introduce the situation; discuss a small reading
goal is easier to keep than an ambitious one with an example; discuss discussing an idea helps us understand it more clearly with a different example;
conclude by connecting the two points.)
